title: Failure
summary: Name timeouts, retries, and idempotency for one hop that will fail.

parts.rule: For each important dependency, set a timeout inside the caller's latency budget and decide which failures are safe to retry. Bound attempts, add backoff with jitter, and make retried writes idempotent. Then state the exhausted outcome: fail, use stale data, fall back, or accept work for later. A timeout limits waiting; it does not prove whether the remote side completed.
parts.why: Distributed failures are often ambiguous. The caller may time out after the server committed a write but before the response arrived. Blind retry can duplicate a charge, while no timeout can hold threads until the service collapses. A useful design connects the client policy to server-side deduplication and a clear user-visible result.
parts.example: Checkout has an 800 ms budget for Billing. Each attempt gets a 200 ms timeout. It retries at most 2 times after timeouts, connection resets, or 503 responses, waiting about 50 ms then 100 ms plus small random jitter. It does not retry a 400 decline. All three attempts carry Idempotency-Key order-781-charge. Billing stores that key with the completed 6000-cent result in the same durable transaction as the charge. If attempt 1 commits but its response is lost, attempt 2 finds the key and returns the original result instead of charging again. The upper bound is roughly 200 + 50 + 200 + 100 + 200 = 750 ms, leaving a little time for Checkout to form its response. After the third transient failure, Checkout marks payment pending or returns a stable unavailable result according to the product contract; it never reports a successful order without knowing the charge outcome. A circuit breaker may fail fast after a sustained high error rate so thousands of callers do not amplify an outage. By contrast, if a cache lookup times out after 20 ms, the read path can fall back to the database. Retry policy depends on the operation: a cheap read and a money-moving write do not share one generic rule.
parts.use: Apply this reasoning to every synchronous network or storage hop on the critical path. Give slower dependencies a share of the end-to-end deadline, retry only transient failures, and require idempotency for side effects. Define fallback data freshness and expose metrics for timeouts, retries, deduplication hits, and breaker state.
parts.refuse: Never rely on an unbounded library default or retry forever in a user request. Do not retry validation errors or non-idempotent writes without a deduplication contract. Avoid layered retries at client, gateway, and service that multiply into a retry storm. “Highly available” is not a failure plan; name what the user sees and what data may be stale or pending.

body:
Rule. For each important dependency, set a timeout inside the caller's latency budget and decide which failures are safe to retry. Bound attempts, add backoff with jitter, and make retried writes idempotent. Then state the exhausted outcome: fail, use stale data, fall back, or accept work for later. A timeout limits waiting; it does not prove whether the remote side completed.

Why it matters. Distributed failures are often ambiguous. The caller may time out after the server committed a write but before the response arrived. Blind retry can duplicate a charge, while no timeout can hold threads until the service collapses. A useful design connects the client policy to server-side deduplication and a clear user-visible result.

Worked example. Checkout has an 800 ms budget for Billing. Each attempt gets a 200 ms timeout. It retries at most 2 times after timeouts, connection resets, or 503 responses, waiting about 50 ms then 100 ms plus small random jitter. It does not retry a 400 decline. All three attempts carry Idempotency-Key order-781-charge. Billing stores that key with the completed 6000-cent result in the same durable transaction as the charge. If attempt 1 commits but its response is lost, attempt 2 finds the key and returns the original result instead of charging again. The upper bound is roughly 200 + 50 + 200 + 100 + 200 = 750 ms, leaving a little time for Checkout to form its response. After the third transient failure, Checkout marks payment pending or returns a stable unavailable result according to the product contract; it never reports a successful order without knowing the charge outcome. A circuit breaker may fail fast after a sustained high error rate so thousands of callers do not amplify an outage. By contrast, if a cache lookup times out after 20 ms, the read path can fall back to the database. Retry policy depends on the operation: a cheap read and a money-moving write do not share one generic rule.

[[diagram:blast]]

When to use. Apply this reasoning to every synchronous network or storage hop on the critical path. Give slower dependencies a share of the end-to-end deadline, retry only transient failures, and require idempotency for side effects. Define fallback data freshness and expose metrics for timeouts, retries, deduplication hits, and breaker state.

When to refuse. Never rely on an unbounded library default or retry forever in a user request. Do not retry validation errors or non-idempotent writes without a deduplication contract. Avoid layered retries at client, gateway, and service that multiply into a retry storm. “Highly available” is not a failure plan; name what the user sees and what data may be stale or pending.
